vignettes.body:
Alex Tay is an analyst researching Buttery Ranch International. Buttery is a Hong Kong SAR-based retail company reporting under IFRS. Buttery and its subsidiaries have fiscal years ending on 31 December. Buttery's functional and presentation currency is the USD.

Tay collects components of Buttery's net sales growth from various markets of the most recent year in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
# Market | Volume Growth | Price Growth | Foreign Currency Exchange
Thailand | 5% | 0% | 4%
Malaysia | 4% | 5% | –4%
Hong Kong SAR | –4% | 8% | 0%

Creamy Meadows is a subsidiary of Buttery. Creamy began operations in Indonesia on 1 January of the most recent year and uses the Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) as its functional currency. Buttery uses the temporal method to translate Creamy's financial results. For the most recent year, Creamy had a net monetary liability and the IDR strengthened against the USD. Tay believes that the translation method may distort the financial and operating measures of the international subsidiary. To verify this, Tay compares Creamy's translated ratios to the ratios calculated under the local currency by using the exchange rates of the most recent year in Exhibit 2

Exhibit 2
# Date | IDR per USD (Amount of IDR per 1 USD)
1 January of the most recent year | 15,000
Average for the most recent year | 14,700
Weighted average rate when inventory was purchased | 14,700
31 December of the most recent year | 14,000

Finally, Tay analyzes another subsidiary of Buttery, Dairy Barn. Dairy uses the local currency of its home market as its functional currency. Buttery used the current rate method to translate Dairy's financial statements in the most recent year. Dairy's home market has been experiencing high inflation and Tay expects it to be classified as a hyperinflationary economy beginning in the current year.

questions.q: The market with the highest sustainable sales growth rate is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: Thailand's organic growth is only 5% + 0% = 5%; 4% came from exchange rates, which is less sustainable.
B. Correct. Sustainable growth comes from volume and price, not exchange rates. Malaysia: 4% + 5% = 9%, above Thailand (5%) and Hong Kong SAR (−4% + 8% = 4%).
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: Hong Kong SAR's volume and price growth is −4% + 8% = 4%, lower than Malaysia's 9%.

questions.q: For the most recent year, as a result of consolidating Creamy's results, Buttery would recognize a:
options: translation loss in the income statement.
translation gain in the income statement.
negative translation adjustment in the balance sheet.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Under the temporal method, a net monetary liability position with the foreign currency (IDR) strengthening produces a translation loss in the income statement.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: the temporal method gives a loss, not a gain, in these conditions.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: a translation adjustment in the balance sheet (equity) arises under the current rate method, not the temporal method.

questions.q: Which of the following ratios for Creamy most likely remains unchanged after translation for the most recent year?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: current assets include inventory translated at the historical rate (14,700) and monetary items at the year-end rate (14,000), while liabilities are at 14,000, so the ratio changes.
B. Correct. Under the temporal method sales are translated at the average rate and COGS at the rate when the inventory was purchased; both are 14,700, so the translated ratio equals the local-currency ratio.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: sales use the average rate (14,700) and receivables the year-end rate (14,000), so the ratio changes.

questions.q: If Tay's expectation is correct, when translating Dairy's current year financial statements, Buttery is required to restate Dairy's:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Under IAS 29 non-monetary items such as inventory (at historical cost) are restated with the general price index before translation at the current rate.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: monetary items such as accounts payable are already in current monetary units and are not restated.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: monetary items such as accounts receivable are not restated.

vignettes.body:
Danny Aoun is an equity portfolio manager at Betterflow Investments. He is developing sentiment indicators for forecasting stock price movements. Aoun gathers textual data from the internet to build machine-learning models. He extracts raw content from a variety of online sources and then trains the models for sentiment prediction. Each text item is labelled as either positive sentiment or negative sentiment. Aoun is more concerned about the models producing false negatives than false positives. He computes selected performance metrics for three models using confusion matrices and presents the metrics in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
# Model | Precision | Recall | F1 Score | Accuracy
X | 0.87 | 0.94 | 0.90 | 0.88
Y | 0.93 | 0.90 | 0.91 | 0.92
Z | 0.96 | 0.82 | 0.88 | 0.86

Aoun then applies his models to determine investor sentiment towards two semiconductor company stocks, Bytewave and Circuitcraft. He also attempts to predict their stock prices using historical data in a regression model.

For Bytewave, Aoun estimates a first-order autoregressive model (AR(1)) on the stock price. From the results, he concludes that the time-series model exhibits autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity and has ARCH(1) errors.

For Circuitcraft, Aoun considers company fundamentals and predicts the growth in quarterly sales. He gathers quarterly sales data for the past 13 years and runs a regression using the first difference of quarterly sales growth in an AR(2) model. After reviewing the first-differenced time-series data, Aoun determines that the mean and the variance are constant over time. Aoun concludes that the time series does not have a unit root. Circuitcraft's historical quarterly sales growth for the most recent quarters has been as follows: Sales Growth50 = 18.9%, Sales Growth49 = 2.0%, and Sales Growth48 = –11.5%. The critical value for the t-statistic in this model is 2.0 at the 5% significance level. Exhibit 2 shows the results from this regression model.

Exhibit 2
Regression Statistics
R2 | 0.2951
Standard error | 0.1270
Observations | 50
Durbin–Watson statistic | 2.2887

# | Coefficient | Standard Error | t-Statistic
Intercept | 0.0024 | 0.0180 | 0.1325
Sales Growtht–1 – Sales Growtht–2 | –0.2021 | 0.1229 | –1.6443
Sales Growtht–2 – Sales Growtht–3 | –0.5272 | 0.1215 | –4.3411

Autocorrelations of the Residual
# Lag | Autocorrelation | Standard Error | t-Statistic
1 | –0.1825 | 0.1414 | –1.2907
2 | –0.0716 | 0.1414 | –0.5061
3 | –0.2606 | 0.1414 | –1.8424
4 | 0.0609 | 0.1414 | 0.4306

questions.q: Which machine-learning model should Aoun choose given his concern about false negatives?
questions.why:
A. Correct. Recall (correctly predicted positives / all actual positives) is the metric to use when false negatives are costly. Model X has the highest recall (0.94).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: Model Y has the highest accuracy and F1 score, which weight false positives and false negatives equally.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: Model Z has the highest precision, which matters when false positives are costly.

questions.q: Based on Aoun's conclusion regarding the time-series model for Bytewave, the variance of the error term is:
questions.why:
A. Correct. With ARCH(1) errors the variance in period t + 1 depends on the squared error of period t, so it is not constant but predictable.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: ARCH errors have a non-constant variance.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: ARCH(1) makes the variance depend linearly on the previous squared error, so it is predictable.

questions.q: The first-differenced time series for Circuitcraft's growth in quarterly sales:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: b2 = −0.5272 is significant (t = −4.34) and less than 1 in absolute value, so it is not a random walk.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: none of the residual autocorrelations is significant (the largest |t| is 1.84 below 2.0), so there is no seasonality (the 4th-lag autocorrelation is not significant).
C. Correct. Residuals are uncorrelated, Aoun found a constant mean and variance and no unit root: the three conditions of covariance stationarity hold.

questions.q: Based on the regression results for Circuitcraft, the 1-period-ahead sales growth forecast is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this forgets to add back the latest growth rate (the regression forecasts the change in growth).
B. Correct. ΔSG51 = 0.0024 − 0.2021 × (0.189 − 0.020) − 0.5272 × (0.020 − (−0.115)) = −0.1029, so Sales Growth51 = 0.189 − 0.1029 = 0.0861, about 8.6%.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this reverses the growth percentages in the formula.

vignettes.body:
Richard Smith is the chief economist at BMT Consulting and is conducting a training program devoted to economic growth. New analysts are organized into teams to analyze various issues regarding the topic. Each team is then required to provide a short presentation of the key points resulting from their discussions.

Smith begins with a framework for explaining the percentage change in stock market value as the sum of three factors: the percentage change in GDP, the percentage change in the ratio of earnings to GDP, and the percentage change in the price-to-earnings multiple.

Smith shows that the growth accounting equation decomposes the percentage change in output into components attributable to capital, labor, and technology. Team Blue is asked to calculate the economy's potential growth rate using the growth accounting method, based on the following information.
Growth rate of capital = 2.0%
Growth rate of labor = 0.5%
Growth rate of total factor productivity = 1.0%
Share of capital in GDP = 30%

Team Green is asked to discuss how investment in physical capital, human capital, and technological development affects economic growth. As a summary of the discussion, Team Green presents a number of points including the following three:
Point 1: Since technology results in an upward shift in the production function, the relationship between economic growth and R&D spending is positive in the short run.
Point 2: Total factor productivity reflects the state of technology, and can be measured by the contribution of capital deepening plus the growth rates of labor productivity.
Point 3: Although long-term sustainable growth cannot rely on pure capital deepening, the impact of investment spending on available capital depends on the existing physical capital stock.

Smith introduces three main paradigms with respect to per capita growth in an economy: the classical, neoclassical, and endogenous growth models. Comparing those models, Smith emphasizes that the factors that drive long-term economic growth are the subject of much debate. Team Yellow is asked to analyze the impact of the various parameters on the steady state in the neoclassical growth model. Team Yellow reports that the following factors permanently change the growth rate of output per worker.
Factor 1: Growth rate of labor force
Factor 2: Growth rate of total factor productivity

Team Purple is asked to investigate whether the per capita income of a developing country should converge toward that of developed countries over time. Team Purple reviews various determinants of per capital incomes: saving rate, population growth rate, the shape of production function, and the externalities associated with human capital. After a debate among team members, Team Purple concludes that the externalities associated with human capital is the most important determinant in predicting the occurrence of convergence.

Smith presents the expected impact of removing trade barriers to economic growth. Referring to the neoclassical growth model, Smith concludes that opening up the economy should increase the rate at which countries' capital-to-labor ratios converge. Team Orange is asked to describe the dynamic adjustment process consistent with Smith's conclusion. Team Orange provides the following descriptions:
Description 1: The growth in the capital-exporting countries will be above the steady state.
Description 2: Developed countries will tend to run trade deficits as they export capital.
Description 3: The rate of return on investments will be lower in countries with high capital-to-labor ratios.

questions.q: Based on the information given to Team Blue, the estimate of the economy's potential growth rate is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Growth = TFP growth + α × capital growth + (1 − α) × labor growth = 1.0% + 0.30 × 2.0% + 0.70 × 0.5% = 1.95%.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: this swaps the weights (70% on capital and 30% on labor).
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this simply adds the three growth rates (1.0% + 2.0% + 0.5%).

questions.q: Which of the points raised by Team Green is most likely correct?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the relationship between R&D spending and growth is not clear-cut in the short run (creative destruction can slow growth cyclically).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: labor productivity growth equals the contribution of capital deepening plus TFP growth, so TFP is not capital deepening plus labor productivity growth.
C. Correct. The impact of investment on available capital depends on the existing capital stock (large in developing countries), even though sustainable long-term growth cannot rely on capital deepening alone.

questions.q: Which of the following convergence concepts is most compatible with Team Purple's conclusion?
questions.why:
A. Correct. Externalities from human capital (endogenous growth) remove diminishing returns, so rich countries can keep their lead; the model makes no prediction that convergence occurs.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: absolute convergence assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital and the same technology.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: conditional convergence also assumes diminishing returns to capital (the neoclassical model).

questions.q: Which of the following descriptions provided by Team Orange is consistent with Smith's conclusion?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: growth in the capital-exporting countries will be below the steady state (capital flows out to the capital-poor country).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: capital-poor countries run trade deficits while developed countries run trade surpluses as they export capital.
C. Correct. Marginal product of capital is lower where capital per worker is high, so returns are lower in high capital-to-labor countries and higher in low capital-to-labor countries.

vignettes.body:
Li Guoqing is a fund manager who is reviewing four similar ETFs. He calculates the expected 1-year holding period cost for ETF 1 based on the information in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
# | ETF 1
Annual management fee | 0.50%
One-way trading commission | 0.10%
Bid–ask spread on purchase and sale | 0.20%

Li believes that the four ETFs share the same factor. He believes that there are arbitrage opportunities among the four ETFs, based on the data in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2
# | ETF 1 | ETF 2 | ETF 3 | ETF 4
Expected return | 2.60% | 3.00% | 3.50% | 4.00%
Factor sensitivity | 0.6 | 1.0 | 1.6 | 2.0

Using arbitrage pricing theory (APT), Li considers the following trading strategies to exploit the arbitrage opportunity:
Strategy 1: Sell short $6 million of ETF 1 and $4 million of ETF 3; buy $10 million of ETF 2.
Strategy 2: Sell short $6 million of ETF 2 and $4 million of ETF 4; buy $10 million of ETF 3.
Strategy 3: Buy $4 million of ETF 2 and $6 million of ETF 4; sell short $10 million of ETF 3.

Li uses a two-factor model to analyze the returns of one of the equity portfolios in his fund. He examines how fund returns, RP, are related to surprises in inflation, FINFL, and GDP growth, FGDP, as shown below:
RP = aP + bP1FINFL + bP2FGDP + εP

Li estimates the expected return of the portfolio to be 1.8% and uses an error term of 0.2%. The actual and expected values of inflation and GDP growth, as well as the estimated portfolio's sensitivities to these factors, are presented in Exhibit 3.

Exhibit 3
# Variable | Actual Value (%) | Predicted Value (%) | Factor Sensitivity
Inflation | 1.2 | 0.8 | 3.0
GDP growth | –3.5 | –4.0 | 0.8

questions.q: Excluding any compounding effects, the expected 1-year holding period cost for investing in ETF 1 is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses a one-way commission instead of round-trip (0.10% + 0.20% = 0.30%; + 0.50% = 0.80%).
B. Correct. Round-trip trading cost = 2 × 0.10% commission + 2 × ½ × 0.20% spread = 0.40%. Holding cost = 0.40% + 0.50% fee = 0.90%.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses the full bid-ask spread twice instead of half the spread each way (0.60% + 0.50%).

questions.q: The most profitable strategy to exploit the arbitrage opportunities is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: Strategy 1 has zero factor risk but earns only $4,000.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: Strategy 2 earns $10,000 but leaves a factor risk of 0.2, so it is not an arbitrage.
C. Correct. Strategy 3 earns $10,000 (4 × 3.0% + 6 × 4.0% − 10 × 3.5% = 0.01m) with a factor sensitivity of 4/10 × 1.0 + 6/10 × 2.0 − 1.6 = 0: the highest return with zero factor risk.

questions.q: Li's two-factor model is best categorized as a:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: statistical models extract factors (portfolios) from historical returns.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: fundamental factors are company attributes (book-to-price, size, P/E, leverage).
C. Correct. The factors are surprises in macroeconomic variables (inflation, GDP growth), so it is a macroeconomic factor model.

questions.q: Based on the two-factor model, the return on Li's portfolio is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this omits the expected return aP (3.0 × 0.4% + 0.8 × 0.5% + 0.2% = 1.8%).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses the actual values instead of the surprises.
C. Correct. RP = 1.8% + 3.0 × (1.2% − 0.8%) + 0.8 × (−3.5% − (−4.0%)) + 0.2% = 1.8% + 1.2% + 0.4% + 0.2% = 3.6%.

vignettes.body:
Xiao Li is a private wealth manager who focuses on fixed income markets.

He is reviewing the term structure of interest rates for his domestic market. Li observes that lender and borrower preferences strongly influence yield curve shape, especially for longer-term maturities. For example, Li has detected that the curve has a persistent dip at the 10-year maturity, and that investors in 10-year bonds are not willing to shift to 8- or 12-year bonds even when yields in those maturities are relatively high.

Li reviews Exhibit 1, which contains current shorter-term government bond spot rates.

Exhibit 1
# Maturity | Spot Rate
1-year | 2.02%
2-year | 2.20%
3-year | 2.38%
4-year | 2.52%
5-year | 2.64%

Using the spot curve, Li computes forward rates. He then forecasts that in three years the 2-year spot rate will equal 2.20%, the current 2-year spot rate, but that the remainder of the spot rate curve will be consistent with current forward rates. Li evaluates what his forecast implies about the valuation of a 5-year zero-coupon bond today.

Li is assisting Client A to select an appropriate investment strategy, who has a 2-year investment horizon. The client expects the yield curve to remain unchanged over the 2-year horizon. Li recommends implementing a ride the yield curve strategy using government bonds for Client A.

Li studies the characteristics and effects of yield curve volatility. He uses the 3.25% monthly standard deviation of the 15-year government-bond yield to estimate an annual yield volatility of 11.26%. Li also calculates key rate durations for various maturities. He concludes that the higher key rate durations associated with longer-term rates leads to higher long-term annualized term structure volatility.

questions.q: Li's observations about the shape of the yield curve are most consistent with the:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: under preferred habitat, investors migrate to other maturities if yields are attractive enough.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: liquidity preference says forward rates are biased by a liquidity premium that rises with maturity, which is inconsistent with borrower and lender preferences shaping the curve.
C. Correct. Segmented markets: investors stay in specific maturity ranges and will not move even when yields elsewhere are more attractive.

questions.q: Given his forecast, Li should consider a 5-year zero-coupon bond today to be:
questions.why:
A. Correct. The forecasted future 2-year spot rate (2.20%) is below the implied forward rate for those last two years, so the bond's cash flows are currently discounted at too high a rate: the bond is undervalued.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: a bond is fairly valued only if future spot rates equal today's implied forward rates.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: it would be overvalued only if future spot rates exceed the implied forward rates.

questions.q: To implement the strategy for Client A, Li should buy a:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: riding the yield curve means buying a maturity longer than the horizon (2 years).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: a 2-year bond matches the horizon and does not ride the curve.
C. Correct. With an upward-sloping curve expected to stay unchanged, buy a bond with a maturity longer than the 2-year horizon (3 years) and sell it at the horizon: it rolls down the curve and earns extra return.

questions.q: Are Li's calculation and conclusion related to key rate duration and term structure volatility correct?
options: No, only his annualized volatility estimate is correct
No, only his conclusion related to key rate duration and term structure volatility is correct
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the annualized volatility estimate is right but the key rate duration statement is wrong.
B. Correct. Annual volatility = 3.25% × √12 = 11.26% is correct. Key rate duration measures price sensitivity to a yield change at one maturity, not how volatile rates are; the volatility term structure typically shows short-term rates more volatile than long-term rates.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the key rate duration conclusion is the incorrect part.

vignettes.body:
Carol McAndrew, an equity analyst, specializes in evaluating manufacturing companies. McAndrew is currently evaluating Acme Industries, a large, diversified manufacturing company that reports under IFRS.

During a recent conference call, Acme management disclosed its intent to raise EUR 40 million to fund new investments by borrowing against Acme's EUR 50 million of receivables. Management indicated that it is evaluating two different options to accomplish this objective:
Option 1: Borrow directly against the receivables of EUR 50 million;
Option 2: Create a special purpose entity (SPE), invest EUR 10 million in the SPE, have the SPE borrow EUR 40 million, and then use the funds to purchase EUR 50 million of receivables from Acme.

McAndrew considers the potential impact of these options on Acme's consolidated debt-to-assets ratio, assuming that Acme will be able to influence the financial and operating policy of the SPE, and will be expected to absorb any losses that the SPE may incur.

Next, McAndrew examines whether there are any accounting warning signs related to the overstatement of Acme's net income. After reviewing Acme's financial reports and industry data for the most recent year, McAndrew makes the following observations:
Observation 1: Receivables growth is lower than revenue growth.
Observation 2: Management compensation is largely tied to financial results.
Observation 3: Depreciable lives of Acme's fixed assets are shorter than those of industry peers.

McAndrew also reviews Acme's Beneish M-scores and Altman Z-scores for the past three years and notes that both scores have steadily declined during this time.

Finally, after making any necessary adjustments, McAndrew uses the following data (in EUR millions) to compute Acme's cash-flow-based accruals ratio for the most recent year:
Net income: 7,050
Operating cash flow: 9,826
Investing cash flow: –8,410
Financing cash flow: 5,390
Average net operating assets: 45,894

questions.q: Acme's consolidated debt-to-assets ratio would most likely be:
options: lower under Option 1 compared to Option 2.
the same under either Option 1 or Option 2.
higher under Option 1 compared to Option 2.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: Acme controls the SPE (influence over policies and exposure to variable returns), so it consolidates it and the balance sheet looks the same as borrowing directly.
B. Correct. Under IFRS 10 / SIC-12, control (influence over financial and operating policy and exposure to variable returns) requires consolidation, so the consolidated ratio is the same under both options.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: consolidation makes the two options identical on the balance sheet.

questions.q: Which observation is most likely a potential accounting warning sign related to the overstatement of net income?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: a warning sign is receivables growing faster than revenue (accelerated revenue recognition), not slower.
B. Correct. Management compensation largely tied to financial results is an incentive for overstating net income: a warning sign.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: depreciable lives that are longer (not shorter) than peers would be the warning sign.

questions.q: The trend in Beneish M-scores and Altman Z-scores most likely indicates that:
options: the likelihood of misreporting and the likelihood of bankruptcy have both increased.
the likelihood of misreporting has increased, but the likelihood of bankruptcy has decreased.
the likelihood of misreporting has decreased, but the likelihood of bankruptcy has increased.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: a falling M-score means less likely manipulation, so misreporting has not increased.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: a falling Z-score means higher bankruptcy risk, so bankruptcy likelihood has not decreased.
C. Correct. A higher M-score (less negative) means more likely manipulation, so a decline means lower misreporting likelihood; a lower Z-score means higher likelihood of bankruptcy.

questions.q: Acme's cash-flow-based accruals ratio for the most recent year is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Ratio = [NI − (CFO + CFI)]/average NOA = [7,050 − (9,826 − 8,410)]/45,894 = 12.3%.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: this leaves out net income and nets all cash flows ([9,826 − 8,410 + 5,390]/45,894).
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this adds the net cash flow instead of subtracting it ([7,050 + 1,416]/45,894).

vignettes.body:
Ulu Bala, an analyst for ValEwe Consulting, has been hired to provide valuations for several firm clients.

Firm A is a rapidly growing automotive parts distributor that has asked Bala to provide an estimated fair value of its common stock. Bala selects the appropriate valuation model based on the following information about Firm A:
The firm's dividend payout ratio has been stable over the last 10 years and is expected to remain stable, regardless of future profitability.
Planned expansion into new markets will require significant annual capital expenditures, which will result in dividends exceeding free cash flow to equity.
Compared with peers, the firm has an aggressive policy with respect to reported earnings, as well as a lower quality of accounting disclosure.

Firm B is a regional utilities provider. Firm B's current stock price is $19.00 and Bala uses the dividend discount model to value the stock. In Exhibit 1, Bala forecasts Firm B's earnings for the next three years. He assumes a required return on equity of 8% and a 60% retention ratio. By the end of Year 3, Bala expects Firm B's stock price to be $21.50. ValEwe's approach is to consider a stock to be fairly valued if its price is within 2% of its estimated fair value.

Exhibit 1
# | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3
Forecasted EPS | $1.27 | $1.62 | $1.91

Firm C is a power generation company. Bala forecasts that Firm C's earnings will grow by 8% per year and the cost of equity will remain at 11% for the foreseeable future. Using the DuPont model and the information in Exhibit 2, Bala estimates Firm C's sustainable growth rate.

Exhibit 2
Last year's EPS | $3.20
Dividend payout ratio | 45.0%
Net profit margin | 11.5%
Total assets/equity | 2.25
Total asset turnover | 0.65

Bala then values Firm C's stock using the Gordon growth model. He evaluates the sensitivity of the stock price from the model under a scenario where both the forecasted cost of equity and the earnings growth rate increase by 50 bps.

questions.q: Which of the following valuation models is most appropriate for Firm A?
questions.why:
A. Correct. Dividends will exceed FCFE because of the expansion capex, which is when a free cash flow model is most suitable.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: residual income relies on good-quality accounting, but Firm A's disclosure quality is lower and earnings aggressive.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the DDM suits stable dividend policies tied to profitability; the stable payout ratio history is not relevant going forward.

questions.q: Based on the dividend discount model, Bala should consider Firm B's common stock to be:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the $19.00 price is only 1.6% above the $18.70 fair value, within the 2% band.
B. Correct. Payout = 40%: D1 = 0.51, D2 = 0.65, D3 = 0.76. V0 = 0.51/1.08 + 0.65/1.08² + 0.76/1.08³ + 21.50/1.08³ = $18.70. The price of $19.00 is 1.6% above, within 2%, so fairly valued.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the price is within the 2% band, so the stock is fairly valued.

questions.q: Based on the DuPont model, the sustainable growth rate for Firm C is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses debt/equity (1.25) instead of total assets/equity.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses the payout ratio (45%) instead of the retention ratio.
C. Correct. g = (1 − payout) × net profit margin × asset turnover × leverage = 0.55 × 11.5% × 0.65 × 2.25 = 9.25%.

questions.q: Under Bala's sensitivity scenario, Firm C's estimated share price is expected to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the spread r − g is unchanged but next year's dividend D0 × (1 + g) rises.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: the numerator increases, so the value is not unchanged.
C. Correct. V0 = D0 × (1 + g)/(r − g): both r and g rise by 50 bps so the denominator is unchanged while the numerator (1 + g) increases, raising the price.

vignettes.body:
Cathryn Kehoe is the senior credit analyst for the State Teachers' Pension Fund. She is conducting credit analysis of an ABS held in the fund's portfolio. The ABS is backed by a large number of short-term credit card receivables that are homogeneous. Each receivable is small relative to the total value of the pool.

Kehoe proposes purchasing a 3-year corporate bond issued by Valisker, Inc. The YTM on the Valisker bond is 2.60%. The bond has a credit rating of AA and a modified duration of 2.82. The relevant portion of a 1-year corporate transition matrix, along with corresponding credit spreads, is presented in Exhibit 1. In the matrix, for example, the probability of an AAA-rated bond becoming an A-rated bond at the end of the year is 1.2%.

Exhibit 1
From/To (Entries are in %)
# | AAA | AA | A | BBB | BB
AAA | 90.0 | 8.6 | 1.2 | 0.2 | 0.0
AA | 2.0 | 88.0 | 8.0 | 1.4 | 0.6
A | 0.1 | 1.5 | 87.5 | 7.5 | 1.0
BBB | 0.0 | 0.5 | 4.5 | 85.0 | 7.0
BB | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.2 | 7.7 | 80.0
Credit spread | 0.65% | 0.95% | 1.20% | 1.80% | 3.60%

The fund owns $5 million of a 7-year senior unsecured bond issued by Gonk Industries. Kehoe recommends the fund buy $5 million of credit protection on Gonk using a 5-year CDS. The CDS has a 5-year senior unsecured bond as its reference obligation. Summary data for the CDS are presented in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2
Credit spread | 4.0%
Duration | 4.5 years
Coupon rate | 5.0%

Two months later, a major accounting scandal is uncovered at Gonk and the firm quickly files for bankruptcy. Gonk has three series of bonds outstanding:
3-year subordinated unsecured bonds trading at 20% of par value
5-year senior unsecured bonds trading at 40% of par value
7-year senior unsecured bonds trading at 30% of par value

questions.q: Based on the characteristics of the receivables backing the ABS, which credit analysis approach is most appropriate?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: loan-by-loan suits non-granular, heterogeneous portfolios.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: portfolio-based suits medium-term horizons with a changing portfolio.
C. Correct. Short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets are evaluated with a statistics-based approach (mean default probability, recovery rate and variance of the portfolio).

questions.q: Based on the 1-year corporate transition matrix, the expected 1-year total return on the Valisker bond is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Price change = −modified duration × change in spread, weighted by the AA ROW probabilities: 0.02 × 0.846% + 0.88 × 0 + 0.08 × (−0.705%) + 0.014 × (−2.397%) + 0.006 × (−7.473%) = −0.118%. Return = 2.60% − 0.118% = 2.48%.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: this leaves out the modified duration (uses only the spread changes).
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses the AA column of the matrix instead of the AA row.

questions.q: The upfront premium the fund would receive for purchasing the CDS protection on Gonk Industries is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this multiplies the credit spread by the notional.
B. Correct. Upfront premium % ≈ (credit spread − fixed coupon) × duration = (4.0% − 5.0%) × 4.5 = −4.5%; × $5 million = −$225,000. The spread is below the coupon, so the protection seller pays the upfront premium to the buyer.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses maturity (5 years) instead of duration (4.5).

questions.q: The cash settlement amount for the fund from the Gonk Industries CDS is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the reference (5-year) bond is not the cheapest-to-deliver; the 7-year senior bond is.
B. Correct. The payout uses the cheapest-to-deliver deliverable of equal or higher seniority than the reference obligation: the 7-year senior unsecured bond at 30%. LGD = 70%; 70% × $5 million = $3.5 million.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the 3-year bond (20% of par) is cheaper but subordinated, so it is not deliverable.

vignettes.body:
Ondrej Knizek is a portfolio manager at a European asset management firm. His portfolio includes fixed income and currency derivatives.

Knizek believes that the market is underestimating the potential for interest rate hikes in Hungary. He is considering buying a 2-year European-style call option on the periodically compounded one-year Hungarian forint (HUF) spot interest rate. He uses the binomial model to calculate the value of the desired call option position. Exhibit 1 shows the 1-year discount factor and the fair value of the options for the respective up and down moves at Time Step 1 (c+ and c-), assuming a risk-neutral probability of 50%.

Exhibit 1
c+ fair value (in HUF) | 4,152,800
c- fair value (in HUF) | 214,800
1-year discount factor | 0.99108

Knizek holds US Treasuries which mature in one month. He wants to use a forward rate agreement (FRA) to lock in the 6-month US interest rate at the time the bonds mature. Knizek refers to the US annualized reference interest rates in Exhibit 2 to calculate the no-arbitrage fixed rate of the FRA.

Exhibit 2
1-month rate | 0.60%
6-month rate | 0.81%
7-month rate | 0.87%

Next Knizek observes an arbitrage opportunity in a Polish government bond. He determines that the bond's 6-month forward price is currently below its fair value. For the first step of the arbitrage trade, he establishes a forward position on the government bonds by purchasing 100 bond forward contracts at a price of 109.30 (percentage of par). Each contract has a notional value of 100,000 Polish zloty (PLN).

Three months later, Knizek calculates the fair value of the forward position. The current forward contract bid price is 108.15 and the annualized three-month interest rate is 0.65%.

questions.q: The value (in HUF) of the interest rate call option position is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this subtracts c− instead of adding it.
B. Correct. c = PV[π c+ + (1 − π) c−] = 0.99108 × [0.50 × 4,152,800 + 0.50 × 214,800] = HUF 2,164,000.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this does not apply the risk-neutral probabilities.

questions.q: The no-arbitrage fixed rate on Knizek's US interest rate FRA is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses the 6-month rate instead of the 7-month rate (the FRA is 1 × 7).
B. Correct. FRA = {[1 + 0.0087 × 210/360]/[1 + 0.0060 × 30/360] − 1}/(180/360) = 0.91%.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this multiplies the two factors instead of dividing.

questions.q: To exploit the arbitrage opportunity on the Polish government bond, in addition to the first step, Knizek should:
options: borrow at the risk-free rate and buy the underlying bond.
borrow at the risk-free rate and short sell the underlying bond.
short sell the underlying bond and invest the proceeds at the risk-free rate.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: that is the cash-and-carry used when the forward price is too high.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: short selling is right, but the proceeds are invested, not borrowed.
C. Correct. The forward price is below its no-arbitrage value, so do a reverse carry arbitrage: buy the forward, sell the underlying short and lend the proceeds.

questions.q: The fair value (in PLN) of Knizek's government bond forward position after three months is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Vt = PV[Ft − F0] = (108.15 − 109.30)/(1.0065)^(3/12) = −1.148 per 100; × 100,000 × 100 contracts / 100 = −PLN 114,800.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: this uses the ratio Ft/F0 − 1.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this reverses the sign of the difference.

vignettes.body:
Martina Friso is a portfolio manager at a pension fund. The fund currently invests in domestic equities and bonds. Friso considers adding real estate to the fund's portfolio.

Friso uses mean–variance optimization to determine the appropriate portfolio allocation to real estate. She considers using either a transaction-based or an appraisal-based real estate index to assess the volatility of real estate returns, the estimation of the Sharpe ratio, and the correlation of returns with the existing portfolio. After considering both index types, Friso chooses the appraisal-based index.

Friso compares two publicly traded real estate companies operating in the retail sector, Perpetua Properties, a REIT, and Rainfall Real Estate, a real estate operating company (REOC). Both companies manage portfolios of retail shopping centers and plan to significantly grow their property portfolios by acquiring undervalued assets.

The key objective of Friso's analysis of Perpetua Properties is to evaluate its sustainable dividend-paying capacity. She considers the following measures of income: FFO, adjusted FFO (AFFO), and net income.

Finally, Friso assesses Perpetua Properties' NAV per share based on the data (in $ millions) in Exhibit 1. Perpetua Properties has 100 million shares outstanding.

Exhibit 1
Appraised value of operating properties | 2,850
Cash and equivalents | 120
Land held for development | 350
Total debt | 1,250

questions.q: Friso's choice of real estate index will most likely result in:
options: higher correlation of returns with the rest of the portfolio.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Appraisal lag smooths an appraisal-based index, so it understates the volatility of real estate returns.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: lower volatility overstates (not understates) the Sharpe ratio.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: the lag also lowers the correlation with other asset classes.

questions.q: Compared to Rainfall Real Estate, Perpetua Properties most likely has:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: REITs are largely exempt from corporate income tax if they distribute income.
B. Correct. A REIT must distribute 90-100% of taxable income, so it has a higher payout ratio than a REOC, which can retain earnings.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: a REOC, not a REIT, can retain earnings for acquisitions.

questions.q: Which of the following measures of income would best meet Friso's key objective in her analysis of Perpetua Properties?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: FFO is not a cash flow measure and ignores the capex needed to sustain income.
B. Correct. AFFO (funds available for distribution) is a cash-focused measure of sustainable economic income after maintenance capital expenditures and is the best indicator of dividend-paying ability.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: net income includes non-cash charges and accounting estimates.

questions.q: The NAV per share of Perpetua Properties is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: this leaves out cash and land held for development.
B. Correct. NAV = 2,850 + 120 + 350 − 1,250 = $2,070 million; per share = 2,070/100 = $20.70.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: this does not subtract total debt.

vignettes.body:
Mary Dines, CFA, is a senior portfolio manager at Prism Wealth Management, a private wealth management firm. Dines was recently hired by Jerry Kagan, a successful software entrepreneur, to manage his investment portfolio on a discretionary basis.

During their initial meeting to set up Kagan's account, Dines proposes using Prism's preferred broker to execute trades. Kagan informs Dines that he wishes to trade through another broker that is owned by a friend. Although Dines knows that Prism's preferred broker would provide better execution, without further discussion she agrees to follow Kagan's wishes and use his broker. Additionally, Dines explains that she will not vote any proxies that would not benefit Kagan's account based on a cost-benefit analysis.

At a subsequent meeting, Dines informs Kagan of the premium services offered by her firm at an additional cost, which include direct access to senior research professionals. Kagan decides not to purchase the premium services. A few days later Prism publishes a report changing its recommendation on Cromwell Inc., a cybersecurity company, to a sell. Shortly after publication Dines sets up calls for her premium clients to have detailed discussions with the senior analyst who authored the report, but she does not set up such a call for Kagan. The next day, Kagan calls Dines and asks her to buy Cromwell shares for his account. Dines knows that Kagan is an expert in the cybersecurity sector from their previous interactions. She proceeds to place the order, without informing him of the firm's recent recommendation change.

Several months later, Kagan meets with Dines to discuss how his account has performed relative to other accounts managed with the same strategy. Dines creates a performance presentation that shows the past five years of return data for the top and bottom deciles of all Prism accounts managed with the same strategy. The presentation also includes a disclosure stating that the performance is shown before taxes and gross of fees.

Kagan is pleased with the performance of his account and decides to offer Dines a bonus equal to 1% of any profits above the 12% annual return target. Dines obtains written permission to enter into this arrangement and then accepts the offer. Additionally, to begin their business relationship on a positive note Kagan offers Dines the use of his luxury yacht over the coming weekend. Dines uses the yacht but does not inform her employer as the offer is not related to the return target.

questions.q: Does Dines violate the Standards in the initial meeting with Kagan?
options: Yes, regarding her proxy voting policy
Yes, regarding the broker for Kagan's account
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: Dines violates Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care by not telling Kagan that his directed broker may not give best execution.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: a cost-benefit approach to proxy voting that is disclosed to the client is acceptable.
C. Correct. In a directed brokerage situation the manager must tell the client he may not be getting best execution; Dines did not, violating Standard III(A).

questions.q: Does Dines violate the Standards in her actions related to Cromwell?
options: Yes, because of her actions related to the buy order for Kagan's account
Yes, because of her actions related to setting up calls with the senior analyst
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: Dines violated Standard III(B) Fair Dealing by not telling Kagan about the changed recommendation.
B. Correct. If a client places an order contrary to a current recommendation, the client should be told of the changed recommendation before the order is accepted. Dines did not tell Kagan the rating had changed to sell.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: fair dealing means not equally; premium clients pay for the calls and the calls came after publication, so there is no violation.

questions.q: Dines violates the Standards in her performance presentation for Kagan with regard to:
options: the disclosure of taxes and fees only.
both the account sample and the disclosure of taxes and fees.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Showing only the top and bottom deciles is not fair, accurate and complete (Standard III(D)); a weighted composite of similar portfolios should be used.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: the disclosure that returns are gross of fees and before taxes is adequate.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect: only the account sample is a violation; the disclosure is fine.

questions.q: Does Dines violate the Standards with respect to either Kagan's bonus offer or the use of his yacht?
options: Yes, with respect to Kagan's bonus offer
Yes, with respect to the use of Kagan's yacht
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect: the yacht is a benefit that can create a conflict of interest and was not disclosed to the employer.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect: the bonus was disclosed and approved in writing by the employer, so it complies with Standard IV(B).
C. Correct. Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements: even non-monetary benefits such as using the yacht must be reported and approved by the employer, even if unrelated to the return target.
